title: AI Chip Design Is Real, Verification Remains the Top Bottleneck
dek: AI can already write RTL autonomously, but the real bottleneck in the entire chip pipeline is verification: it consumes more than half of development time, and AI still cannot answer "what to test." OpenAI's twenty-person team can shorten the front end, but the back end still has to be left to humans.
why: The author uses first-hand observations and the words of frontline engineers to rescue "AI making chips" from clickbait: which are prototypes, which can go into production, and where the real barriers lie.
who: Semiconductor investors, chip company decision-makers, and engineers focused on AI implementation who want to judge whether "AI chip design" is a real inflection point or just fundraising rhetoric.
skip: The opening EDA terminology primer (first minute); those familiar with the chip design flow can skip it directly.

points.h: K3 has only a front end, no back end
points.body: The raw material for the "AI 48-hour tapeout" claim is a small inference accelerator called Nano KPU, announced by Kimi: 238,000 parameters, about 1.46 million standard cells, 0.277MB SRAM, claiming to close timing at 100 MHz within 4 square millimeters and decode throughput of 8,700 tokens/s. But the host looked closely: this RTL only underwent functional verification, with no cell placement, routing, physical verification, or sign-off; the so-called "timing closure" relies on estimates, and 100 MHz is not impressive in an open-source 45nm library—human designers using the same library can achieve 20-450 MHz, and commercial processes can reach 1-3 GHz. K3's goal is not to make a good chip but to prove that an agent can autonomously reach functional completeness.

points.h: AI writing RTL is not news at all
points.body: Many people think AI writing chips started with K3, but as early as 2020, NYU used GPT-2 to generate beginner-level RTL, with reports of 94.8% accuracy; the now-defunct eFabless held AI design contests, and Will Salcedo's GPT-4-generated design actually went to tapeout—one of the earliest known LLM-designed tapeouts to the host. "AI writing RTL" itself is not innovative; the real change is that an agent can run unattended from scratch to functional completeness—autonomy in the workflow has been refined.

points.h: The future of agents lies in wrapping toolchains
points.body: When fully autonomous design is still out of reach, the real product form is to wrap LLMs around EDA toolchains: LLMs command deterministic EDA tools via interfaces like MCP or APIs, just as Claude Code lets models call computer tools. Synopsys, Cadence, and Siemens all have long-term goals of opening their stacks, handing data feedback and control to agents that can run for hours or overnight. Siemens demonstrated at Semicon Taiwan: an agent dropping hundreds of standard cells one by one into a simulator, measuring load, speed, and power for later design lookup tables. Switching process nodes means redoing this tedious work, perfect to hand to AI before leaving work.

points.h: Even the best results still require a human in the loop
points.body: Former xAI engineer Christina Lee's post is the most convincing breakdown the host has seen. Her meta-harness has two layers: the inner layer lets the model call EDA tools to write RTL, synthesize, place and route, and verify; the outer layer lets the model review what went right and wrong in the previous round, propose improvements, and run again. The first phase only did a MAC multiply-accumulate array, iterating from 900 MHz to 1 GHz over multiple rounds; the second phase connected the MAC to SRAM and other modules, and complexity immediately rose. Note that humans have always held the steering wheel: so-called goal strings are likely provided by the outer model as a reference, but the selection and final confirmation authority remain with humans. AI is not the boss; it is the co-pilot.

points.h: What is truly scary about Jalapeno is the 20-person team
points.body: OpenAI's Jalapeno demo made many people focus on "RTL to tapeout in just 9 months." The host reminds us: Synopsys has previously said in unrelated contexts that with their tools, without AI, it also takes about 9 to 12 months; the chip is not complex, and the starting point is unclear—the architecture concept only began in October 2024. What really stands out is the team size: only 20 to 30 people stood up at the end of the talk. Moreover, this group's token consumption consistently ranks at the top of OpenAI's internal leaderboards, and the RTL was still being modified the day before the freeze. If such a small team can do it, the number of people needed for chip roles in the future could drop by an order of magnitude—perhaps that is why they do not emphasize it in the slides.

points.h: Verification is the bottleneck for AI chip design
points.body: The whole industry talks up the front-end RTL but glosses over the back end: OpenAI's presentation slides spend a lot on spec and RTL, while the back end—the host guesses—is handled by partner Broadcom, thanked only on slide 34; Lee also hands the back end to Yosys/OpenLane. The mechanistic asymmetry is that PPA (power/performance/area) optimization is a closed loop—generate, verify, measure PPA—AI has a clear reward signal; verification is not. Passing or failing a test does not tell AI how far it is from full coverage, and "what to test" still depends on humans. Chip bugs cannot be changed once taped out, so seeing a defect on the first look at TSMC's silicon is the most crushing moment. This explains why verification can consume 50 to 70% of development time, and echoes Shibo Chen's remark that "AI does design, humans do verification" is what makes people comfortable.

points.h: The biggest enemy of front-end wrappers is OpenAI
points.body: Silicon Valley is spawning numerous startups that wrap frontier models with proprietary knowledge to write RTL. The risk the host sees: Anthropic and OpenAI themselves both own models and are making chips; if they decide to open up their chip-specific models, the differentiation of front-end wrappers disappears. So he prefers to look at teams moving toward the back end and verification, where end-to-end provides a moat. How fast is this field moving? While he was writing, Architect Labs announced that its Redwood chip was fully produced and verified by AI, with specs written only by two architects; even TSMC's 3D IC talk used "agentic AI." The host worries that within a week or two, his judgment could be overturned by new news.

terms.def: Electronic design automation: the software tools needed to design chips, dominated by a few vendors like Synopsys and Cadence.
Register-transfer level: the hardware language layer (Verilog/VHDL) that describes data flow and logic; the "code" of a chip.
Process design kit: the confidential process parameter package maintained jointly by foundries and EDA vendors, tightly protected by NDA.
Power, performance, area: the three key metrics for evaluating chip design quality, directly usable for closed-loop optimization.
The step of handing the fully verified design data to the foundry to manufacture the real chip.
